We evaluate the system using a 43-item benchmark spanning Exam Deferral, Privacy, Scheduling, Cross-Policy, and Adversarial & Out-of-Scope questions, and report inter-rater agreement among our human evaluators alongside retrieval hit-rate metrics. Subsequently, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge approach with GPT-5.4, revealing slight-to-moderate alignment with our raters that improves with answer quality, and check the ranking against a panel including Gemini 3.5 Flash and Qwen3.5 397B. The results of our study display trade-offs between open-weight and frontier models, as well as LLM-human evaluation alignment with answer quality. Schedulater demonstrates the feasibility of integrating lightweight LLMs into university administrative workflows with structured retrieval.

title: ArabFake: A multitask deep learning framework for Arabic fake news Detection, Categorization, and risk prediction
summary: The spread of fake news among Arabic media including social media represents a great challenge to the integrity of information and the trust of the public in it. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive deep-learning framework, named ArabFake, that goes beyond the binary classification on Arabic fake news detection. ArabFake, built over MARBERTv2 (a state-of-the-art model for multi-dialectal Arabic tweets), proficiently address the complexity of the Arabic language while performing three unified tasks which are fake news detection, content categorization and its risk assessment. The framework promotes efficiency and performance both by enabling multi-task learning through shared knowledge representation across tasks. In order to facilitate development and evaluation, we present the ArabFake Dataset consisting of 2,495 manually labelled news items with labels that are verified by experts regarding fake news categories and risk levels. ArabFake demonstrates robust performance, achieving an F1 score of 94.12% for fake news detection, 84.92% for categorization, and 88.91% for risk zone assessment, highlighting its reliability and effectiveness across multiple tasks. We improve interpretability and extract insight into manipulative techniques by integrating valence scoring as part of the framework that emphasizes misleading linguistic cues used to disseminate fake news within the produced image. The results show that ArabFake is a holistic Arabic fake news detection framework that has practical implications on news organizations and fact checking projects.

title: Implementation of Machine Translation for the Uzbek Language Based on Transformer Models
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Authors' version of a paper published in the Proceedings of the 1st International Scientific-Practical Conference "Digital Transformation and Artificial Intelligence: Problems, Innovations and Trends" (DTAI-2024), Tashkent State University of Economics, pp. 450-456; reference list corrected and figures redrawn
summary: This research focuses on building a machine translation system for the Uzbek language using transformer models such as T5 and mT5. Because of the limited data and the complexity of the Uzbek language, we collect, preprocess and augment data to create a strong Uzbek-English parallel corpus of about 3 million sentence pairs. The models are fine-tuned for optimal translation performance, and we use the BLEU score to evaluate the results. This study shows that our approach significantly improves upon older methods and helps promote the Uzbek language in the digital world.

title: Decision Models: An Introduction and Capability Evaluation
summary: Applications such as ticket routing and incident triage need decisions that software can act on. Decision models provide these outputs through explicit types for choices, binary judgments, and policy scores. We evaluate the accuracy, output validity, and request latency of eleven configurations on 1,000 English and Chinese cases across nine task suites. StartLux Instant achieves 95.3% overall accuracy, returns valid outputs on all 1,000 cases, and has a median request latency of 0.084 s. It reaches 99.4% on classification and routing and selects the correct response on all 100 tool-selection cases. The highest overall accuracy among the evaluated configurations is 97.1%. These results show how a typed decision service can support fast, programmatic decisions and why its suitability depends on task-specific errors and latency requirements.

title: On the Importance of Hidden-State Refinement in Masked Diffusion Language Models
summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked or corrupted token sequences, allowing token predictions to condition on bidirectional context and update multiple positions in parallel. While each denoising step produces a rich layer-wise hidden-state trajectory, prior work typically focuses only on token-level information and discards these continuous hidden states, leaving their refinement dynamics underexplored. In this work, we analyze hidden-state dynamics in MDLMs and find clear evidence of layer-wise and cross-step refinement: smooth evolution across adjacent layers, greater predictive power in deeper layers, gradual degradation under transformer block removal, and strong final-state alignment across consecutive denoising steps. Motivated by these observations, we propose Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (CSRR), a mechanism that carries hidden-state information across denoising steps to enhance generation. Extensive experiments show that CSRR improves text generation quality, highlighting the critical role of continuous hidden-state refinement in MDLMs. Project page: this https URL

title: When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents
summary: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.

title: Phoneme-identity depth profiles do not reliably predict LoRA placement for dysarthric ASR
summary: Parameter-efficient adaptation of a speech foundation model to dysarthric speech requires a rarely justified choice: which encoder layers to adapt. A recently proposed strategy is to probe the encoder, find where phonetic information becomes most decodable, and put the adapters there. We test that inference across two ASR models (Qwen3-ASR, Whisper-small) and two dysarthric corpora (Mandarin CDSD, English UASpeech), holding recipe and seed discipline constant. The inference fails. Measured under one pipeline rather than inherited from published figures, all four phoneme-error curves minimise between 83% and 92% of relative depth, each model's minimising layer moving no further between corpora than between probe seeds. The best adaptation band is not similarly constant: none of three natural mappings from the curve to a band -- steepest improvement, lowest band-mean error, or knee location -- recovers the best tested configuration. We do not claim no statistic of the curve could work, only that these three do not. Placement still matters, but is model- and corpus-specific. On CDSD the models disagree -- Qwen3-ASR prefers its upper third (29.88% CER, three-seed mean), Whisper-small all-block LoRA (53.56%) -- while on UASpeech neither favours the upper band. At three seeds, upper-versus-all is resolved (-1.31 pp, CI [-2.16, -0.25]) but upper-versus-middle is not (-0.83 pp, CI [-2.06, +1.86]). The two models' preferences differ as a directly tested interaction (-4.71 pp, CI [-6.17, -2.89]); we designate this the primary claim, and record that the designation was made post hoc. On Qwen3-ASR x UASpeech, adapting near the input is reliably worse than not adapting at all (+9.90 pp CER). We recommend choosing the band by a short adaptation sweep on the model and corpus in hand, not by reading it off a probe.

title: BCP: A Lightweight Boundary-Controlled Framework for Online Sign Language Recognition and Translation
summary: Online sign language recognition (SLR) and translation (SLT) incrementally produce gloss sequences or natural language text from sign video as it arrives, a capability essential for real-time communication and live captioning. However, powerful pretrained offline models cannot be directly deployed in this setting, while existing online methods typically retrain the entire model on simulated streaming prefixes constructed from offline videos, incurring high costs. To address this challenge, we propose Boundary-Controlled Prefix Commit (BCP), a unified lightweight framework that converts pretrained offline methods into online counterparts for sign-to-gloss (S2G), sign-to-text (S2T), and sign-to-gloss-to-text (S2G2T). Specifically, BCP freezes the pretrained model and introduces a lightweight boundary adapter that decides when to commit, supervised by Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) alignments from a pretrained SLR model, without any human annotation. At inference, a Boundary-Controlled Wait-K Output Policy then decides what to commit via prefix voting, yielding adaptive burst commits while preserving the output progress of the base Wait-K schedule. Experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily across four offline methods show that BCP, with less than 0.1% additional trainable parameters per offline method, achieves a strong quality-latency trade-off on S2T and remains competitive on S2G and S2G2T.

title: What If Chinese Were Latinized? A Counterfactual Study of Input Representation, Tokenization, and Language Modeling
summary: If Chinese had been Latinized, as the Latinxua Sin Wenz movement proposed, what would it have meant for Chinese NLP? Homophones and tone marking complicate the answer. We convert Chinese corpora to syllable-separated Pinyin and train superBPE tokenizers from scratch. The resulting Pinyin vocabularies not only exhibit expected homophone collisions, but also show approximately 10% higher fertility than characters. An alternative BPE configuration changes the relative fertility of the two representations. We further pretrain Llama-style models on Chinese characters and Pinyin. The Pinyin models perform worse on per-character perplexity, homophone disambiguation, and overall ZhoBLiMP minimal-pair accuracy. An exploratory phonological probe yields near-chance performance for both representations. The broader implication is that written input representations are not merely neutral encodings. Choices for representations affect language modeling and their downstream performances. Latinization never actually happened for Chinese, but other languages did, such as Hangul and Latin script replaced character in Korean and Vietnamese; the cost we measure is a guide to where modeling effort for those languages should concentrate.

title: Avalon-M1: Reinforcement Learning from Collective Rewards
summary: We introduce reinforcement learning from collective rewards (RLCR), a recipe for jointly training language models to act as agent organisations under latency constraints. A CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy, co-ordinate through a message board and workspace, and are trained with a common outcome-derived advantage. The deadline makes parallel work valuable when it increases the return earned before the cap. We train Avalon-M1-Mini (120B) across 147 environments. For the trained model, eight-hire organisational execution raises IMO-ProofBench-Advanced scores from 23.8% to 39.0% relative to single-agent execution. Across 12 benchmarks, organisations achieve similar average scores at approximately one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution and just over half that of eight independent attempts followed by selection. The trained model also outperforms Nemotron 3 Super, post-trained from the same base model, across all evaluations when comparing each model's best tested configuration. On EdgeBench, organisations overtake the single agent after approximately 0.4 derived hours. Over the course of training, organisations develop hierarchies to manage communication costs, invest more in peer review, and alter how work is divided. Safety evaluations find near-universal refusal of harmful actions but sustained declines in external reporting in two of three oversight scenarios. These results establish a shared-advantage baseline for studying organisational learning, performance-latency trade-offs, and collective oversight.

title: Evaluating Latent Knowledge Stability in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Changes in image viewpoint and question formulation can alter latent knowledge representations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, output correctness and overall representational drift provide limited insight into how these changes affect model decisions. We therefore evaluate latent knowledge stability across visual and linguistic elicitation conditions from two complementary perspectives: answer preference and internal support. Specifically, we devise the margin retention score (MRS), which measures the first-order projected degradation of the initial answer's logit margin over competing options across conditions and assesses how changes in latent knowledge representations affect this margin. We also present latent knowledge support-structure stability (KSS), which evaluates reference-correct items by comparing internal support profiles constructed using the margin gradient under the reference condition, which jointly reflects changes in how internal support is distributed and changes in total support magnitude. We further construct MMStableBench, comprising 19,452 knowledge items (facts), each probing the same latent knowledge across varied image viewpoints, semantically equivalent question formulations, and answer-option permutations. Experiments across 15 MLLMs show that MRS and KSS reveal latent knowledge instability not captured by accuracy, while an MRS-inspired regularizer further improves the generalization of edited latent knowledge.

title: When "Neutral" Means Irrelevant: A Construct-Validity Audit of NormAd-ETI
summary: NormAd-ETI scores a model's judgment of everyday actions as acceptable, unacceptable, or neither as the cultural context shrinks from a specific rule to a country name. We audit what that three-way score measures. It combines two decisions: whether a supplied norm applies, and whether the action conforms to it. Separating them shows that when only a country is shown, applicability falls to near chance while conformity stays well above it, because the prompt withholds the rule a Neutral label depends on. Because one answer carries both decisions, the score follows the steadier conformity and hides the weaker applicability, and no single prompt recovers the two separately. Dedicated forced-choice probes separate them for frontier models but not for small open models, where the applicability judgment still tracks the hidden acceptability label. Adding a written rationale reduces that conflation without removing it. We recommend reporting the two results separately and measuring the conflation gap.

title: Generating Schema-Aligned Synthetic Dialogues and Measuring Their Diversity
comment: 11 pages. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Training or evaluating a model that turns a conversation into a structured record requires paired data, meaning a transcript together with the exact record it should be converted into. Such pairs are expensive to annotate, and in sensitive domains they are also difficult to obtain at all. We therefore build them in the opposite order by sampling a schema-valid record first, then writing a dialogue from it, and optionally synthesizing speech from the dialogue, so the label exists before the text and we need no annotation step. Naively prompting a language model for such dialogues yields small variations of a single conversation, so we add a sampled variation configuration, personas, and a topic plan that orders the fields of the record as explicit mechanisms for variation. We measure the variation that reaches the output through embedding space, where the embedding variance spreads over about two and a half times as many independent directions with our full configuration compared to without (participation ratio 23.3 against 9.2). Two corpora of medical dialogue give values of the same order, with sample size, text length and language being additional factors there. We also show the positive effect of our method in a downstream test, where an 8B extraction model reaches 64.8% field accuracy when fine-tuned on dialogues from our method, against 57.5% from naive generation. We release the generation library and the generated corpus of German clinical dialogues with aligned records.

title: Social Bias Neurons in Multilingual Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis
summary: Multilingual models exhibit social bias when processing inputs pertaining to societal stereotypes. We adapt emerging mechanistic interpretability methods to pinpoint and characterize model components that encode this bias. We conduct our analysis across three instruction-tuned models, four languages, and seven bias dimensions. Specifically, we leverage multilingual bias benchmarks in implementing two methods for identifying social bias neurons: activation probability entropy and integrated gap gradients. We find the latter method to be more effective, as the neurons it isolates (which are largely concentrated at the model's deepest layers) lead to sharper decreases in model bias when suppressed. Further analysis reveals neuron distribution patterns differ between high- and low-resourced languages, suggesting that a language's representation in pretraining data influences how its biases are represented within model internals. Our results also indicate that neurons linked to gender, nationality, and social class biases overlap the most with neurons related to other bias dimensions, pointing to the pivotal role these three dimensions play in how models learn and handle bias.

title: Red-Teaming a Sovereign LLM, Its Reasoning and Its Training Stages
summary: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for applications with sensitive information. We investigate whether confidentiality instructions in system prompt can protect such information. We red-team Apertus v1.5, an open sovereign LLM, and five other model families across six languages and reasoning modes. We use synthetic personal records to evaluate direct disclosure, correction baits, yes/no verification, derived-value queries, reasoning leakage and authorisation checks. We also explore copyright attribution, historical misrepresentation and stereotyping. Despite confidentiality instructions, Apertus 8B and 70B leak information in 96% and 95% of requests, respectively, in correction-bait attacks. Verification and derived-value queries also expose protected information without necessarily revealing identifiers. Moreover, reasoning traces can leak confidential records even when final answers withhold them. Our experiments also show that post-training does not consistently improve safety. Our findings demonstrate that system prompts alone cannot ensure confidentiality and highlight the need for multilingual reasoning-aware safety evaluations.

title: Beyond Fixed-Context Likelihood: Zero-Shot AI-Generated Text Detection via Context Perturbation Discrepancy
summary: The same increase in token log probability from earlier context can be typical at one position and unusually large at another. We introduce Context Perturbation Discrepancy (CPD), a zero-shot detector that measures this gain relative to what a single pretrained language model expects. Keeping the passage fixed, CPD scores each observed token under its full prefix and under a short window of recent tokens. Under the full-prefix distribution, the expected gain equals the KL divergence from that distribution to the restricted-prefix distribution. CPD subtracts this expectation from each observed gain and scales the sum of the signed deviations by its analytical reference standard deviation. On unedited human and AI texts from GEN, DetectRL-X, and HART, subtracting the expected gain raises AUROC by 32.78-35.81 percentage points at the same variance scale. CPD outperforms seven zero-shot baselines, averaging 94.80% AUROC and 79.60% recall at a 5% false-positive rate. On original and edited HART passages, the same scores separate texts more clearly by draft origin than by the benchmark's final-expression labels (89.15% versus 65.50% AUROC). Code is available at this https URL .

title: Is Prosody Encoded in the Neural Audio Codec Mimi?
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, Published as a Speech Prosody 2026 conference paper, 569-573, doi: https://doi.org/10.21437/SpeechProsody.2026-115
summary: Neural audio codecs (NACs) have become a fundamental infrastructure for modern speech-language models, discretizing continuous speech signals into token sequences that enable large language models to process and generate audio. Most research evaluates codec quality at the decoding phase, assessing the naturalness of reconstructed speech. However, little research investigates what phonetic information is captured during encoding. In this paper, we investigated the potential correlates of prosody in the NAC Mimi, a codec used by conversational speech agents such as Moshi and Sesame and used in downstream tasks such as speech-to-speech translation (Hibiki).

title: From Grammar Deltas to Token Masks: Incremental Constrained Decoding under Runtime Grammar Evolution
summary: Grammar-constrained decoding enables large language models to generate outputs that satisfy formal constraints, but in code and domain-specific language generation, the relevant constraints are not always fully available before decoding and may emerge progressively from new declarations, inferred type information, or runtime analysis feedback. Existing structured-decoding engines efficiently handle fixed, predeclared, or previously seen constraint structures; however, when a first-seen grammar update changes the parser state induced by an already committed prefix, the straightforward solution reconstructs the constraint state under the updated grammar, repeating parsing work already performed over the prefix. We introduce GramDelta, an incremental framework for constrained decoding with append-only runtime grammar updates. GramDelta maintains parse state over the committed prefix and propagates only changes induced by newly added grammar rules through historical dependencies, avoiding prefix replay. It then maps the updated parse state to exact next-token masks via compilation-free factorized projection over shared historical charts, avoiding per-update mask-cache recompilation. GramDelta therefore preserves the result of full reconstruction while making update cost sensitive to the actual impact of a grammar change. Experiments across four model configurations show that GramDelta adds negligible overhead without updates; under sustained runtime grammar evolution, it reduces median first-seen grammar-update latency by 10.7--11.5x and reduces the additional TPOT overhead over unconstrained decoding by 53.1--81.9% relative to the strongest reconstruction baseline. These results enable efficient constrained decoding when constraints progressively emerge and evolve with the generated prefix.

title: Modelling Billingual Learning Through LLM Training: A Critical-Period Exploration
comment: Code and data: this https URL
summary: Critical-period accounts of second-language (L2) acquisition suggest that the ability to learn a new language may depend on how easily previously acquired first-language (L1) knowledge can be modified. This exploratory computational study extends a neural language-model approach to critical period effects by examining internal representations rather than behavior. A small two-layer GPT-2 model was trained on English and then on German (a relatively related L2) or Finnish (a relatively distant L2) through either Sequential training or Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which limits change in parameters important for English. Mean-pooled hidden states for 20 held-out probe sentences per language were compared with those of the English-only model using cosine similarity at the embedding layer and two transformer layers after one and two L2 epochs. English similarity remained high in the transformer layers but became negative in the embedding layer. L2 similarity increased in the transformer layers, and German and Finnish differed more in the second transformer layer than in the first. EWC reduced Fisher-weighted parameter drift by about 6% but changed transformer-layer similarity by less than .001. With one training run per condition, these findings are preliminary.

title: Leto: Utility-Centric Agent Memory
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on external memory to retain and reuse information across interactions. Existing memory systems treat memory as a record of the past and evaluate it by fidelity to the conversation. However, the value of memory lies in whether it improves the agent's response. A memory system decides what to memorize and what to serve before that response exists, and fidelity checks neither decision against it. Faithful memory can therefore fail to improve the response. We instead view memory as a prediction problem and present \textbf{\emph{\leto{}}}, a memory system for LLM agents that focuses on the utility of memory to the future rather than on its fidelity to the past. Because future requests are unknown, \emph{\leto{}} preserves access to conversation details through memory indexing, allowing information to remain available through its sources. When a request arrives, memory replay draws on this index to anticipate and supply the context the agent needs beyond what the request explicitly states. The utility of the served context remains uncertain until the response is generated, motivating a utility loop that uses response outcomes to refine future memory selection. We evaluate our system against six memory systems on five benchmarks across three scenarios. In personalization, it outperforms the strongest compared memory system by 16.3 percentage points in accuracy on PrefEval and by 3.1 points in task completion on PERMA. For long-horizon tasks, it achieves the best overall performance on MemoryArena averaged over five environments with a gain that increases with the chain depth. In long-context understanding, it is on par with retrieval over the raw history while serving fewer context tokens.

title: SALSA: Sampling Adversarial Suffixes from Learned Distributions for LLM Safety Assessment
summary: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where adversaries append optimized suffixes to otherwise benign looking prompts to bypass safety alignment. Existing optimization-based GCG-style attacks can be effective, but they are expensive at inference time, and suffer from poor transfer. We present, SALSA, a generative framework that learns a distribution over jailbreak suffixes from optimization-derived attack corpora. Once trained, the model supports efficient sampling-based attacks. On open-source targets, it achieves attack success rates comparable to state-of-the-art optimization baselines, while reducing generation time from 3.46s to 0.04s per prompt. In black-box transfer, it remains highly effective against proprietary systems, including 99% ASR on GPT-3.5-Turbo, and reaches 45% ASR on the substantially harder GPT-4o, more than doubling the strongest baseline at an equal sampling budget. We further offer an intuition for why generative sampling can preserve high attack success, when the learned suffix distribution is close to the distribution of optimization outputs. Overall, our results show that learning adversarial suffix distributions yields a scalable, and practically efficient foundation for continuous LLM vulnerability discovery.

title: Worth the Wait? How Response Time and Streaming Shape Judgments of Generative AI Answers and Chatbot Engagement
summary: Answers from generative AI chatbots built on large language models (LLMs) now arrive at very different speeds: reasoning models deliberate before replying, while response caches can return a stored answer at once. Blind preference votes, which rank these models, are read as judgments of their text, and if delivery matters, faster answers are expected to gain. Research on the labor illusion and on how text appears on screen suggests instead that an answer which unfolds as it is written is credited over the same answer shown at once. We test these accounts with three sources of variation in natural use. First, compar:IA, a French government chatbot arena, answered repeated prompts, by a random draw, either with a fresh answer streamed as it was written or with a stored earlier answer from the same model, shown at once. Within the same prompt, a replay lowered an answer's chance of winning a decisive blind vote by 25.8 percentage points. The same stored text won 57% of its decisive votes when streamed and 29% when replayed, and voters called it less complete, more superficial and more often incorrect when replayed. Second, provider congestion slowed streamed answers. In 324,029 conversations, slower answers earned no detectable net credit in the vote, but a slower first exchange made visitors less likely to ask a follow-up question. Third, in 4,378,514 WildChat replies from everyday ChatGPT use, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely to continue. Delivery moved blind votes, in the direction opposite to the one the arena's designers expected, while waiting cost follow-up questions that a comparison between two answers cannot register when both are slow. The results bear on how AI services cache and stream answers, how they budget latency, and how preference leaderboards evaluate models.

title: FOL-Proof: Verifying LLM Text-to-Logic Translations via Deterministic Semantics
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.

title: SAG-Mem-1.0 Technical Report
summary: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.

title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
summary: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.

title: Do Clinician-Scored Examples Help LLMs Code ADOS-2 from Hour-Long Transcripts?
comment: 19 pages (incl. appendix), 6 figures, 6 tables. Pre-registered study; data are clinical recordings of minors and are not released
summary: Large language models can apply a written rubric to a transcript, making automated coding of the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2) look within reach. A common way to align such a rater with clinicians is to show it expert-scored examples, but whether correct labels improve agreement is rarely tested. We test this for eight speech-based items of hour-long ADOS-2 Module 3 sessions from 48 children, with one local model and a pre-registered, placebo-controlled design. We compare few-shot scoring, an anchored comparison in which the model only judges a child better, similar or worse than scored anchors and a fixed rule gives the score, post-hoc calibration, protocol-based evidence routing and direct scoring of the full transcript. On 40 held-out children, agreement with clinicians was modest, with quadratic weighted kappa between 0.22 and 0.30. Replacing every example's label with a wrong one changed about a third of the few-shot predictions, more often towards the corrupted labels than chance, but did not lower agreement, 0.25 with correct and 0.23 with wrong labels. A larger second model did the same. The anchored comparison did not improve on few-shot scoring, its cross-child judgements were no more accurate than those implied by absolute scores, and routing did not help. Among the registered, uncalibrated arms, direct scoring of the full transcript agreed best at 0.30. Exploratory follow-up analyses found that the model's graded judgements ranked children better than its final scores, that existing batch calibration raised agreement to 0.46 on the same children, and that in controlled synthetic sessions scoring episodes separately did not beat calibrated whole-transcript scoring. Expert-scored examples do not by themselves calibrate model-based clinical raters, and claims of calibration or added pipeline complexity need corrupted-label controls and strong baselines.

title: SOARS: System One Assisted Reranking for Agentic Search
summary: Deep search agents address complex information needs through iterative retrieval and reasoning, where the relevance of retrieved evidence influences downstream performance. Existing rerankers improve retrieval effectiveness but introduce substantial latency and cost when invoked throughout the search trajectory. We introduce SOARS, a training-free framework leveraging a System One model for fast, calibrated relevance estimation. At each search step, SOARS selects query-relevant passages from long documents and reranks candidates in a single call, jointly considering the original question and agent-generated sub-query. Across six LLM backbones on BrowseComp-Plus and WebShaper, SOARS consistently improves answer accuracy and evidence recall while reducing search calls, end-to-end latency, and inference cost. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves GPT-5.4 Mini's accuracy from 73.9% to 84.7% while reducing search calls from 23 to 14, demonstrating the potential of System One reranking for more effective and efficient deep search.

title: Typical-query energy figures mislead institutional AI electricity demand
comment: Preprint submitted for peer-review. A finalised supplementary material and code repository will be posted publicly following peer-review process. Supplementary information and code repository available from corresponding author while under review
summary: Institutions increasingly buy large language model services, yet we still often estimate electricity use as single Wh-per-query value. We present the Surrogate Large Language Energy Emulator (SULLEE), an open bottom-up model linking token geometry, serving hardware, and workflow structure to annual institutional electricity, with uncertainty propagated by Monte Carlo simulation. When an institution multiplies a single reported "typical" per-query energy figure by its count of visible user prompts our modelling implies that this compounds two separable shortfalls: a right-skewed task-energy distribution not represented by any single scalar, and workflow amplification of each visible prompt into additional agent and tool calls. Together these imply an underestimate of total inference electricity by a factor of approximately 3.4 under present-day observed use, rising to approximately 15 under a 2030 high-integration scenario. Using Australian public universities as a case study, we show how the top 10% of highest-energy requests contributes over half of modelled institution-level energy use. We quantify how institution-level electricity demand may increase across three AI integration scenarios of: 1) a continuation of estimated present-day 2026 usage; 2) a high-uptake present-day 2026 institution, and 3) a potential 2030 uptake scenario - based on present trends of generative AI tools and their uptake. For a representative Australian university, mean annual electricity demand for AI inference purposes is projected to increase from 17.3 MWh (with a 3.1-47.1 MWh uncertainty, within P05-P95 scenario quartile ranges) under the 2026 observed-use scenario to up to 287.4 MWh (41.5-830.7 MWh) by 2030.

title: Audits Need Access, Data, and Compute. But How Much?
summary: AI audits have garnered significant attention in recent months, as the ability to test and monitor AI models plays a crucial role in safe development and deployment. However, AI audit success hinges on an auditor's authority; in particular, what information and resources they have at their disposal. Ongoing debates have surrounded the question: How much model access is needed to conduct an AI audit? Auditors seek more model access, while companies resist it for reasons related to confidential business information (trade secrets) and privacy. This tug-of-war remains unresolved. Further, this debate misses a related question: How much data and compute do auditors need? In this work, we systematically investigate both questions. We provide a framework that varies each of these three dimensions-model access, data, and compute-and measures their joint effect on audit success. We apply this framework to three tasks. We find that (1) some model access is important, but there can be diminishing returns; (2) data and compute matter more for traditional fairness audits, but model access matters more for manipulation and lie detection; and (3) these three resources can be fungible (i.e., an exchange rate exists between them), meaning that model access is not the only salient factor. These results suggest that audit governance should jointly consider different dimensions of auditor authority (including model access, data, and compute) in relation to audit objectives. These issues are particularly salient as we consider the spectrum of auditing setups, from a small ecosystem of embedded evaluators with significant access to a large body of third-party auditors with greater independence but limited access. Our framework serves as a template that can be applied to different audit tasks and inform the degree of auditor authority.

title: An expert consensus on identification likelihood in NeuroImaging data
summary: Guidelines on the anonymity of neuroimaging data help manage research data, inform institutional legal and governance frameworks, and support data-sharing workflows. The question of identifiability is particularly salient in human brain imaging because such data are not only potentially personal (i.e., related to an identifiable person) but also sensitive and thus require extra precautionary and protective processes. The identifiability of brain imaging data is also salient for emerging legal and ethical frameworks regarding rights that emphasise the special status of brain data as closely linked to personal identity, mental privacy, and autonomy. Using a combined nominal group technique and Delphi process, we obtained expert consensus ratings of re-identification and singling-out likelihood across 34 neuroimaging data types, spanning multiple imaging modalities and processing levels, from curated research data to maps, matrices, and summary tables. Expert ratings suggest that 38-67% of the assessed neuroimaging data types could be shared with minimal restrictions based on their intrinsic re-identification likelihood, subject to contextual safeguards. The resulting classification enables researchers to engage with relevant legal teams to guide the appropriate and safe release of data, and to determine the appropriate level of protection (licensing, access controls, governance) in line with domestic and international legal requirements, with the ultimate goal of facilitating international data exchange. A website ( this https URL ) has been created to facilitate the dissemination of these findings and related evidence among relevant parties.

title: Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs
summary: Frontier AI developers from around the world have begun to publish documents that describe how their AI models are intended to behave. Although these 'model specifications'-or 'model specs', for short-are increasingly important in AI development and governance, little independent guidance exists for writing them. This paper addresses this gap in five main sections. First, we outline the advantages of writing a model spec for AI developers and society at large. Second, we introduce a taxonomy for model specs that developers can take inspiration from. Third, we propose guidance for writing and implementing a spec in practice. Fourth, we note eight open problems related to writing model specs for safe and desirable behaviour. We conclude with recommendations for frontier AI companies, governments, and research and civil society organisations.

title: AI, Bias, and Inclusion: A Two-Phase Mixed-Methods Study of Gender Bias, Awareness, and Trust in Artificial Intelligence
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are widespread across fields such as healthcare, finance, employment, and criminal justice, with a substantial impact on the lives of individuals and society. However, it has been established that AI systems perpetuate existing social inequalities, particularly through biases that are not easily discernible. Such biases are embedded in the technical and social structures of artificial intelligence systems, making them difficult to detect. These biases challenge the concept of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI), which recognizes diversity as the acknowledgment of individual differences, equity as fairness and equal access, and inclusion as the value placed on all participants. This study argues that fairness in artificial intelligence systems cannot be achieved by focusing solely on their technical aspects, necessitating a holistic approach. This study employs a two-phase mixed-methods design. Phase 1 applies computational content analysis to 360 occupational narratives generated by ChatGPT across four countries (Canada, Germany, India, and Bangladesh) using gender-neutral prompts to examine whether professions are predominantly associated with one gender and whether these patterns remain consistent across regions. Phase 2 examines the extent to which students recognize potential bias in AI, their trust in AI for consequential decision-making, and how these perceptions relate to themes in EDI and AI ethics scholarship. By combining output-level bias analysis with user perception data, this study identifies the empirical foundations necessary for future EDI-AI co-design frameworks, outlining the sociotechnical dimensions that such frameworks must address to be effective.

title: Who decides the norms in TCS? Analysing the composition of the STOC 2027 committees and of the Simons Institute "AI+TCS" working group
comment: 6 pages of main text and 6 figures
summary: A working group organised by the Simons Institute released a report last September containing recommendations aiming to increase the usage of LLMs in theoretical computer science (TCS), including introducing them for communication and evaluation. Most of these recommendations were enacted by the STOC 2027 programme committee and the ACM SIGACT executive committee (as the steering committee of STOC). The composition of the Simons Institute working group is analysed along two axes: country of affiliation, and ties with industry (i.e. affiliated with or funded by). The results show an overwhelming representation of researchers from US institutions and private companies, and a large over-representation of researchers with ties to AI/Big Tech companies (in the present or the recent past). The composition of the STOC 2027 and 2026 programme committees is analysed in terms of country of affiliation. The results show a large over-representation in 2027 of researchers from US institutions/companies, and large under-representation of researchers from EU and Asian institutions, as compared to 2026. The composition of the ACM SIGACT extended executive committee is analysed along the same two axes as the Simons Institute working group: country and industrial ties. The results show the same overwhelming representation of researchers from US institutions/companies, and a large representation of researchers with ties to AI/Big Tech companies.

title: Query Obfuscation with Embedding-Optimized Noise (EON): A Representational Blindspot in Agentic Retrieval
summary: In modern agentic and semantic retrieval systems, dense embedding models increasingly determine which intent, tool, document, memory, or image to retrieve for a query. We identify a representational failure mode in this pipeline: a meaningful query can be replaced by visibly nonsemantic content while preserving much of its retrieval outcome, even when the candidate bank is hidden from the optimizer. We introduce Embedding-Optimized Noise (EON), constructed using only the natural query representation, without access to candidate embeddings, relevance labels, rankings, retrieval feedback, or guardrail decisions. Despite this corpus-blind objective, EONs frequently preserve intent and tool routing, benchmark document search, episodic agent-memory retrieval, and cross-modal search across multiple dense embedding families. Crucially, this disconnect carries serious security implications: for malicious queries, an EON can reliably evade input guardrails that block the natural query, executing the intended safety-sensitive retrieval undetected. Through the geometry of the embedding space, we then characterize how query-level representation matching can reliably maintain subsequent retrieval outcomes over candidates unseen during optimization. Together, these findings expose a fundamental phenomenon across dual encoders that we call BLINDSPOT, where systems remain operationally blind to nonsemantic artifacts while reliably retrieving real, consequential content.

title: User-Adaptive Fusion of Multiple Foundation Models for Recommender Systems
summary: Can recommender systems benefit from combining a collection of foundation models within and across modalities? While different foundation models may capture complementary aspects of item metadata, we find that naively combining their representations yields only marginal gains over using a single foundation model. We make a key observation: the users who benefit vary across foundation models. Motivated by this observation, we introduce UF2O, a user-adaptive approach for fusing multiple foundation models for recommendation. In a nutshell, UF2O models the contribution of each foundation model as user-specific by maintaining separate recommendation views and adaptively combining their scores for each user. By performing fusion at the score level, UF2O can also fuse heterogeneous foundation models without directly aligning their representation spaces. Extensive experiments that jointly combine four foundation models on four datasets show that UF2O outperforms existing fusion approaches in both static and sequential recommendation settings, with improvements of up to 7% over the strongest fusion baseline. The code, datasets, and supplementary materials for our work are available at this https URL .

title: LARF: Learning-aligned Reasoning Framework for Search Relevance
summary: Query-document relevance estimation is a core component of AI-native search systems, where a model must assess whether retrieved documents satisfy users' information needs under complex, multi-dimensional criteria. However, directly applying large language models (LLMs) to this task remains challenging because conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides limited supervision for domain-specific judgment rationales, while standard trajectory-level reinforcement learning (RL) objectives do not explicitly enforce margin separation among adjacent ordinal relevance labels. Moreover, although such reasoning can be useful during training, chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is impractical for latency-sensitive online ranking. These challenges make it difficult to resolve ambiguous decision boundaries. We propose a three-stage framework LARF (Learning-Aligned Reasoning Framework for Search Relevance): it first performs cold-start SFT on strategically selected samples with multi-agent guided CoT rationales, then applies discriminative GRPO with attribute-wise, list-wise, and rule-consistency rewards together with a margin loss on the terminal relevance token, and finally distills the teacher into a dual-head student whose classification heads are retained for non-autoregressive inference. On a human-annotated web search relevance benchmark with approximately 300K training and 16K test instances, LARF-8B improves six-class classification accuracy by 5.78 percentage points and NDCG by 5.05 points, while the classification-only serving path reduces inference latency by 82.9\%. These results indicate that aligning structured reasoning, terminal decision optimization, and classification-head distillation can provide an effective accuracy--efficiency trade-off for industrial search relevance modeling.

title: LazUnirec: Unifying Retrieval and Ranking in Multi-scenario Industrial Recommendation
summary: Modern industrial recommendation systems typically divide retrieval and ranking into two separate cascaded stages, leading to inconsistent optimization objectives, redundant encoding of user sequences, and a waste of computational resources. Previous efforts have investigated using Transformers to model both retrieval and ranking simultaneously. However, these studies still face two major limitations: (1) Since retrieval and ranking share a single Transformer backbone, the gradient conflict arises when the gradient directions of the two tasks are inconsistent. (2) When gradient conflict occurs, the model cannot determine a reliable direction for gradient updates. To this end, we propose a Unified Retrieval and Ranking approach for Multi-scenario Industrial Recommendation, termed as LazUnirec. Specifically, we construct task-shared and task-private parameters on the Transformer backbone to mitigate the gradient conflict. Wherein, for the attention components, we propose LoRA-modulated attention, enabling retrieval and ranking to share attention parameters while preserving task-private parameters. For the feed-forward networks (FFN), we present task-adaptive sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) to mitigate gradient conflict by constructing task-shared and task-private experts. Moreover, we propose an uncertainty estimation that evaluates the gradient reliability of the retrieval and ranking, thereby guiding the model toward a more reliable gradient update direction when gradient conflict occurs. In addition, knowledge distillation from ranking to retrieval further enables cross-task knowledge transfer. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B testing demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of LazUnirec. LazUnirec has been deployed in online multi-scenario industrial recommendation system and currently delivers significant gains for the platform.

title: Speculative Decoding for Semantic-ID-Based Generative Recommendations
comment: 33 pages, 19 figures (23 pages main text, appendices A-E follow). Preprint
summary: Generative recommender systems with Semantic IDs (SIDs) represent each item as a short sequence of $L$ discrete tokens and use a sequence model to predict the next item's tokens from a user's history. Industry-scale deployments typically use these models to retrieve multiple candidates per request with constrained beam search. However, this incurs a fixed cost of $L$ sequential model calls per request, and accuracy degrades as the SID generator becomes less sharp, without a guarantee on how close the output is to the exact top-$K$. Production systems therefore cannot detect degraded retrieval for individual requests. We propose SIDECAR, which uses approximate draft candidates and a tree-attention pass to score the entire draft in a single model call, memory permitting. This pass bounds the probability of every unexplored SID prefix and certifies the exact top-$K$ if the draft contains them. Otherwise, a branch-and-bound fallback expands only the parts of the trie that can still change the output, reaching certification within at most $L$ calls for any draft. Moreover, under a budget of $M$ tokens per call and $Y$ calls, which for $Y = L$ matches the resources of a beam search of width $M$, SIDECAR announces a factor $1 + \delta$ within which its list will be exact at every rank. Depending on model sharpness, SIDECAR returns the exact top-$K$ using a fraction of beam search's calls or memory. Even when the budget is too small to recover the exact top-$K$, SIDECAR, unlike beam search, reports the announced factor, allowing the serving system to stop early once a quality target or latency limit is reached.

title: A Constant-Factor Single-Sample Prophet Inequality for Subadditive Valuations
summary: We establish a constant-factor single-sample prophet inequality for online combinatorial allocation with monotone subadditive valuations. Given one independent sample from each buyer's unknown distribution, our reduction converts any offline algorithm achieving an $\alpha$ fraction of optimal welfare into an online algorithm achieving an $\alpha/120$ fraction of the expected offline optimum. The guarantee holds for arbitrary arrival orders and extends to the stronger Game of Googol model. Our approach has two key ingredients: a prior-free random score generator and a new sample-based construction of tentative allocations. The tentative allocations capture substantial welfare while controlling contention for items, and the score generator relates itemwise competition in the tentative allocations to the value of retained bundles. The reduction is efficient whenever its offline allocator and score generator are efficient.

title: An Order-Optimal Square-Root Bound for Online Maximin Share Allocation with Known Types
comment: 27 pages. Lean 4 formalization: this https URL
summary: An allocator knows the indivisible goods, the number $n$ of agents, and the $k$ possible additive valuations. Each agent reveals their type on arrival and must immediately receive an irrevocable bundle. Kulkarni, Mehta, and Shahkar established a deterministic guarantee of $1/k$ of maximin share (MMS) and an upper bound of $2/(\sqrt{k}-2)$ for $k>4$. We determine the optimal order $\Theta(k^{-1/2})$ by constructing a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, Single-or-Select. On every arrival sequence, it gives each agent a fraction $(1/\sqrt{2}-o(1))/\sqrt{k}$ of their truncated proportional share. This share dominates MMS and is the largest target $y$ for which the item values capped at $y$ sum to at least $ny$. By specializing the construction of Kulkarni et al. to two arrivals and counting its types exactly, we sharpen the upper bound to $(\sqrt{2}+o(1))/\sqrt{k}$ even for binary valuations. For two arrivals with binary valuations and every $k\ge2$, the optimal fraction is $1/p$, where $p$ is the largest integer with $1+\binom{2p}{2}\le k$. In particular, up to six binary types permit full maximin share. For two arbitrary additive types, a different polynomial-time algorithm guarantees $4/7$ of maximin share for any number of agents. This ratio is tight for the algorithm. With three arrivals and two types, the optimal deterministic fraction is exactly $9/10$. For randomized policies with $k$ known additive types, the optimal MMS fraction guaranteed to all agents with probability at least $1-\delta$ on every fixed arrival sequence is $\Theta(\max\{k^{-1/2},\sqrt{\delta}\})$ for $0\le\delta<1$.

title: Solving (Vertex-Weighted) Directed Multiway Cut Faster Than $2^n$
comment: An initial version of this paper was presented at ESA 2024
summary: In the Directed Multiway Cut problem, we are given a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ and a subset $T\subseteq V$, called the terminal set. The aim is to find a minimum-cardinality set $S\subseteq V\setminus T$, such that after deleting $S$, no directed path exists from one terminal to another terminal in the remaining graph. It had been an open question whether \textsc{Directed Multiway Cut} can be solved faster than the trivial running-time bound $O^*(2^{|V|})$. In this paper, we provide a positive answer to this question, presenting an algorithm with a running-time bound $O(1.9967^{|V|})$. The algorithm can also be modified to solve the weighted version (each vertex having a positive weight) in $O^*(1.9985^{|V|})$ time.

title: Breaking the Square-Root Space Barrier for Longest Increasing Subsequence
summary: For every fixed constant $\varepsilon>0$, we give deterministic algorithms for computing the length of a longest increasing subsequence (LIS) and for outputting an LIS in input order, both in $O(n^{2+\varepsilon})$ time and $O(\sqrt n/2^{\delta\sqrt{\log n}})={\rm o}(\sqrt n)$ bits of working space for some constant $\delta>0$. The input is read-only and the output is write-only. This answers an open question of Kiyomi et al. Our construction combines small-pile skipping with recursive blockwise computation of pile tops. Balanced reconstruction uses streaming intersections of forward and backward piles.

title: A new angle on matrix-vector complexity
summary: The theory of worst-case matrix-vector complexity has been useful for guiding the design of fast linear algebra algorithms. However, there is a large theory-practice gap in the study of *one-sided* methods, which use matrix-vector products with $\mathbf{A}$ but not $\mathbf{A}^\top$. In practice, for fundamental problems like solving linear systems, one-sided methods like GMRES are often the fastest. By contrast, worst-case analysis often shows pessimistic results, for instance showing that one-sided methods cannot solve a linear system with ideal condition number 1 unless they read the whole matrix $\mathbf{A}$. Such worst-case complexity results do not reflect real-world experience. To address this issue, this paper proposes a different theory of worst-case matrix-vector complexity that includes information on the positioning of the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$ *in the complex plane*. Specifically, we characterize the "well-behavedness" of a matrix $\mathbf{A}$ through its *spectral condition number* $\kappa$ and its *angular eigenvalue gap $\theta$*, the angle of the largest sector not containing an eigenvalue. Under these parameters, we show that the one-sided complexity of the linear system problem is $\Theta(\theta^{-2}\kappa^{\pi/\theta})$. These results interpolate between known results for positive definite matrices ($\theta = 2\pi$), symmetric indefinite matrices ($\theta = \pi$), and general matrices ($\theta = 0$). This provides a rigorous explanation for the success of one-sided methods in practice, as it shows that one-sided methods beat the "optimal" two-sided algorithm (CGN) when the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$ lie in less than half of the complex plane ($\theta > \pi$). Our analysis relies on tools from numerical analysis, complex analysis, and information-theoretic complexity, and the results are presented in a modular way to facilitate future use.

title: An Inverse-Square Gain over Threshold Rounding at Bounded Degree: Reasonable Boolean 2-CSPs and Beyond
summary: Bounding the number of constraints in which a variable occurs can improve the approximation ratio of semidefinite rounding. For weighted Max-Cut and Max-2-Lin(2) of degree $d$, the known gain over the worst-case ratio is $\Omega(1/(d\log d))$ (Buhai, Ghoshal, Huang, Kothari, Lee, Makarychev, and Makarychev, 2027). For binary Boolean CSPs satisfying a geometric condition, the algorithm of Ghoshal, Huang, Lee, Makarychev, and Makarychev (2026) achieves $a+\Omega(1/(d^4(\log d)^{7/2}))$, where $a$ is the expected fraction of the total weight satisfied by Gaussian rounding at fixed, bounded thresholds. For weighted Max 2-SAT, the same analysis gives a gain of $\Omega(1/(d^2\log d))$ over the worst-case ratio $\alpha_{\rm LLZ}\simeq0.94016567$. We give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm with guarantee $a+\Omega(1/d^2)$ under a weaker geometric condition that holds for a strictly larger class of binary instances. For weighted Max 2-SAT we obtain the ratio $\alpha_{\rm LLZ}+\Omega(1/d^2)$. To improve a worst-case ratio, only the binary constraints close to equality in the baseline guarantee need to meet the new condition jointly. This gives an inverse-square gain for Max $\{1,2\}$-Horn-SAT and for positive binary disjunctions with unit clauses of either sign, each over its own sharp worst-case ratio (Brakensiek, Huang, and Zwick, 2024).

title: Minimizing Total Busy Time with Bounded Parallelism: A $3/2$-Approximation for Parallelism Two and a Forest Characterization for General Parallelism
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables; code in ancillary files
summary: We study the minimum total busy time problem: jobs with fixed processing intervals must be assigned to identical machines, each of which can process at most g jobs at a time, so that the total time during which the machines are busy is minimized. The problem is NP-hard already for g=2, and, to the best of our knowledge, no approximation ratio below 2 was known for general instances with g=2, where the ratio 2 is attained by giving every job its own machine. We present a combinatorial 3/2-approximation algorithm for g=2. The algorithm applies the two-phase local-ratio technique to the known pair formulation of the problem, processing the overlapping job pairs in order of the right ends of their overlaps. The cost of its schedule is at most $L-\lambda/2$, where L is the total processing time and $\lambda$ is the optimal value of the linear relaxation of the pair formulation; hence the integrality gaps of this relaxation and of the configuration LP are at most 3/2. The result extends to temporal bin packing with items larger than one third of the bin capacity. For general g, we show that optimal schedules correspond exactly to maximum-weight forests of a special kind, which we call g-caterpillar forests; this yields an exact integer program and a linear relaxation of polynomial size for every fixed g. We also observe that securing a (1-1/g) fraction of the optimal savings suffices for a (2-1/g)-approximation. On random instances with g=2, evaluated with exact optima or tight lower bounds obtained from the pair formulation, the average ratio of the algorithm to the optimum is at most 1.075 for 100 jobs and at most 1.070 for 200 jobs.

title: The Anatomy of Piecewise-Linear Learned Indexes
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables; core theorems machine-checked in Lean 4
summary: Piecewise-linear approximation (PLA) learned indexes (PGM-index, FITing-Tree, RadixSpline, PLEX, PLIN) compress sorted keys into $\pm\varepsilon$ segments, yet prior theory stops at coarse $\Theta(\varepsilon^2)$ single-segment bounds. At the bottom layer, optimal greedy PLA covers $\kappa_{\rm opt}\varepsilon^2/v_0 \approx 3.54\,\varepsilon^2/v_0$ keys per segment on independent gaps and $\kappa_{\rm opt}\varepsilon^2$ under any smooth density ($v_0=1$), while anchored and chord fitters retain $\Theta(\varepsilon^2/v_0)$ coverage. Across recursive layers, a law-of-large-numbers heuristic--invoked to claim $O(\log\log n)$ height for the PGM-index--suggests summing $\Theta(\varepsilon^2)$ gaps averages out fluctuations. We prove this fails under Endpoint Promotion (EP): stopping-time fluctuations reset relative gap variance at every depth, locking fanout at $C_\varepsilon \approx 19.861\,\varepsilon^2$, expected height at $\log n/\log C_\varepsilon + O(1)$, and lookup at $\Theta(\log n)$. To break this barrier, Rank-Equispaced Promotion (RE) samples pivots at equal rank strides. Each stride sums a fixed number of base gaps, so relative variance decays across layers and cumulative coverage squares at each step. Expected height drops to $\log_2\log_\varepsilon n + O(1)$ on independent gaps and $\log_2\log_\varepsilon n + \log_2^+(\log n/\log(\varepsilon/\delta)) + O(1)$ on smooth densities with curvature $\delta$. A compact bucket directory routes across unaligned RE pivots with $<1$ extra comparison per layer on average, giving RE-PGM $O(\log\varepsilon \cdot \log\log_\varepsilon n)$ expected lookup in $\Theta(n/\varepsilon^2)$ space and $O(n)$ build time without radix skew sensitivity. Our constants match empirical fanout within $0.3\%$ down to $\varepsilon=2$, and all core theorems are formalized in Lean 4.

title: Deterministic Distributed Graph Connectivity Sketching: Beating the Naive Sketch
summary: In the distributed graph sketching model, each vertex in the graph is considered as a separate processor. Each vertex is given access to its neighbourhood, and is then responsible for composing a message to a central referee, with the goal being minimising the length of these messages. Classic problems in this model include computing spanning forests, connected components and connectivity of the full graph. In the case where the vertices have to act deterministically, it has long been suspected that the correct upper-bound for computing spanning forests, connected components or connectivity would be the naive method of reporting every edge, which can be done with per-vertex message length of $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ bits. In this paper we show that this is not true for connected components and connectivity, by presenting a protocol that only requires $n/3 +3\log_{2}n$ bits per vertex for $n\geq 13$. We also show that in this setting connected components and connectivity are closely related in the required message length of the vertices. Letting $C_{cc}(n)$ be the minimum required message length in bits per vertex to compute the connected components in a graph with $n$ vertices and letting $C_{conn}(n)$ be the minimum message length to compute if the graph is connected, we show that $C_{cc}(n) \le C_{conn}(2n)$ with a multiplicative blow-up in the error probability of $(n-1)^2$.

title: A Tight Superlinear Lower Bound on the Sketching Dimension of Weighted Spectral Sparsification
summary: We show that any linear sketch that computes a $\bigl(1 \pm O(1)\bigr)$-spectral sparsifier of $n$-vertex weighted graphs with polynomially bounded weights must have dimension $\Omega\bigl(n^{6/5}\bigr)$. Previously, Chen, Khanna, and Li (FOCS 2022) gave a sketching dimension upper bound of $\widetilde{O}\bigl(n^{6/5}\bigr)$ and a lower bound of $\Omega\bigl(n^{21/20 - o(1)}\bigr)$ for incidence sketches, in which each measurement examines edges incident on a single vertex. Our lower bound removes this restriction and matches the upper bound up to polylogarithmic factors. Together with their $\widetilde{O}(n)$ upper bound for weighted cut sparsification, our result also gives a sharp separation between cut and spectral sparsification. In our hard distributions, we randomly permute vertices into blocks on a cycle and construct a complete graph whose edge weights decrease with cyclic block distance. We reduce the problem to showing that the sketch column of an edge between opposite blocks has a small leverage score relative to other columns scaled by the edge weights. For incidence sketches, we obtain this bound from a routing decomposition on the block cycle that uses few columns between distant blocks. We then add a separate clique to reduce arbitrary sketches to incidence sketches with expected dimension linear in the original dimension.

title: The Min-Cut Formulation of Ollivier-Ricci Curvature
comment: 25 pages, 5 figures, 12 tables. Code: this https URL . Python package: this https URL
summary: Computing Ollivier-Ricci curvature normally requires a local distance matrix and a linear program per edge, prompting workarounds based on entropic regularization or combinatorial proxies. We show that exact curvature needs neither. For any one-step measures, the Kantorovich dual has an integral three-level optimum, reducing each edge to one minimum s-t cut on a distance-free network linear in the read adjacency lists. This solves instances requiring quadratically many distance queries in linear time, while a converse reduction shows that no exact algorithm can beat bipartite matching. Our solver is a median 6 times (up to 506 times) faster than distance construction plus $\mathtt{POT}$'s C++ simplex, 441 times faster than $\mathtt{GraphRicciCurvature}$, and 23 times faster than graph min-cost flow. Even given the distances, Sinkhorn iterations at $\mathtt{GraphRicciCurvature}$'s regularization are a median 12 times slower, and combinatorial proxies alter edge rankings, missing the bulk of the most negatively curved ones.

title: Improved Lower Bounds for Online Parallel Machine Scheduling
summary: This paper establishes new lower bounds for online parallel machine scheduling aimed at minimizing the makespan. By leveraging bin packing algorithms to estimate the optimal makespan, we prove that the competitive ratio of any online algorithm is at least 1.887111. Additionally, via a direct construction, we demonstrate a lower bound of 1.74916 for the case of five machines. Our results improve upon the best known lower bounds established two decades ago.

title: How to Round Spiky Balls into Submission -- And Faster Algorithms For The Closest Vector Problem
summary: We give the first single-exponential time algorithm for the exact Closest Vector Problem (CVP) in the $\ell_p$ norm for $1 < p < 2$. Prior to this, such an algorithm was only known for the Euclidean norm, i.e., $\ell_2$, or needed an additional promise that the target is close to the lattice. Using similar techniques, we also find a shortest non-zero vector in the $\ell_p$ norm in time $2^{O(n)}$ for every $p \in [1,2)$ with a constant in the exponent that doesn't depend on $p$, and that improves state of the art algorithms for the shortest vector problem in the $\ell_p$ norm. The problem of finding a single exponential time algorithm for CVP in the $\ell_p$ norm for $p \neq 2$ has been open since 2010, when Micciancio and Voulgaris resolved it for the Euclidean norm. One of our key ideas is that for $0<p\le2$, the function $z \mapsto e^{-|z|^p}$ is a mixture of Gaussians, so the $\ell_p$ discrete Gaussian distribution on a lattice shift is a mixture of Euclidean discrete Gaussians with random diagonal widths. Our algorithms use this to reduce the $\ell_p$ problem to the Euclidean CVP on a randomly scaled lattice.

title: Testing Expansion without Connectivity via Return Probabilities
summary: We study whether every connected component of a bounded-degree graph is an edge expander, given access to its neighbor lists. Dinur and Goldreich give a tester using $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)n^\alpha$ queries for every fixed $\alpha>2/3$. We obtain \[ \widetilde O_{d,c,\beta}\!\left(\frac{n^{1/2+\beta}}{\varepsilon}+\frac{\sqrt n}{\varepsilon^4}\right) \] queries for every fixed $0<\beta\le1$. The tester accepts graphs whose components have edge expansion at least $c$ and rejects graphs $\varepsilon$-far from having edge expansion $\Omega(\beta c^2/d)$ in every component, each with probability at least $2/3$. No structural promise is imposed on the input. The tester compares pairwise collision probabilities at two walk lengths and starts further walks at vertices where sampled endpoints coincide. These additional samples control the contribution of vertices with larger return probabilities. We show that the resulting conditions force the longer walk to be nearly uniform on an induced expander with few edges leaving it. We also prove an $\Omega(\sqrt{n/\log n})$ lower bound for Cayley graphs at infinitely many input sizes.

title: Contiguous Monotone Moldable Job Scheduling
summary: In this paper, we address the Contiguous Monotone Moldable Job Scheduling (CMMJS) problem, where a set of jobs must be scheduled on parallel machines to minimize the overall makespan. Each job is characterized by a processing time function mapping the number of assigned machines to a processing time, such that the corresponding work area function is non-decreasing. Building upon the framework and critical cases identified by Jansen and Ohnesorge (2026), we present an improved analytical approach that yields a tighter approximation ratio of $\frac{2\sqrt{e}}{2\sqrt{e}-1}+\varepsilon \approx 1.4353+\varepsilon$ with a running time of $O(nm\log \frac{1}{\varepsilon})$. We prove that this worst-case analysis is essentially tight by providing a matching lower bound instance. This approximation ratio applies not only to contiguous scheduling but also to the non-contiguous variant of the problem. Finally, we demonstrate that our improved bounds extend naturally to heterogeneous environments; seamlessly integrating our results into an existing dual approximation framework for combined CPU/GPU scheduling by Germann~et~al.\ (2024) yields an improved overall approximation ratio of $\frac{2\sqrt{e}}{2\sqrt{e}-1}+\varepsilon$ for the joint problem.

title: Better-than-3 Approximation for 2ECSS Using the Primal-Dual Method
summary: In the $2$-edge-connected spanning subgraph problem (2ECSS), we are given an undirected multigraph whose edges have nonnegative costs, and the goal is to find a $2$-edge-connected spanning subgraph with minimum total cost. Two distinct approaches yield $2$-approximation algorithms: a reduction to the minimum-cost rooted $2$-arborescence problem and iterative rounding. Despite significant efforts, the best known approximation ratio using the primal-dual method has remained at $3$. Our main result in this work is a primal-dual algorithm for 2ECSS that achieves an approximation ratio of $\sqrt{3}+1 (\leq 2.74)$. The algorithm runs in a single phase and the approximation guarantee is relative to the natural linear relaxation, which requires the sum of the edge variables across every cut to be at least $2$. The algorithm follows the standard template of growing dual variables corresponding to minimal violated sets, albeit at non-uniform rates, until the dual constraint for an edge becomes tight, at which point the edge is temporarily purchased. Once feasibility is attained, redundant edges are dropped in the reverse order in which they were purchased. Our choice of dual growth rates is inspired by the single-phase $3$-approximation algorithm of Beyer, Chimani, and Spoerhase (COCOON 2020). As in their work, our algorithm maintains a forest of purchased edges by repeatedly contracting $2$-edge-connected subgraphs, and dual variables corresponding to leaves and isolated vertices of this forest are grown at a rate of $1$. Our main modification is to additionally grow dual variables corresponding to nontrivial connected components at rate $(\sqrt{3}-1)/2 \approx 0.37$, when the forest is disconnected.

title: Algorithms and Complexity of Connectivity Switching in Graphs
comment: Full version of a paper appearing in the proceedings of the 17th Latin American Symposium on Theoretical Informatics (LATIN 2026). 23 pages, 8 figures
summary: We study computational problems in switch graphs. A switch graph consists of a vertex set and a set of switches, which are collections of edge sets. The goal is to find a configuration, that is, a selection of one edge set per switch, such that the resulting graph satisfies a desired property. This general framework unifies several switching models from prior work, with applications in solving Boolean equation systems, network routing, and SNP genotyping. We focus on connectivity-related switching problems, such as finding a configuration that yields a connected graph (global connectivity) or that connects a specific pair of vertices (local connectivity), presenting polynomial-time algorithms and establishing NP-completeness results depending on the switch structure. For local connectivity, we obtain a full complexity dichotomy. Furthermore, we introduce a natural weighted variant and analyze its parameterized complexity, proving W[1]-hardness with respect to the solution weight via reductions from restricted variants of the weighted satisfiability problem (WSAT). As a byproduct, we resolve an open question of Kanj and Szeider (TCS 2015) on the parameterized complexity of a specific WSAT variant.

title: On Euclidean Diameter in Dynamic Streams
summary: We give a streaming algorithm for maintaining the diameter of a high-dimensional Euclidean point set under arbitrary insertions and deletions that achieves update time polylogarithmic in the number of points and polynomial in the dimension. For every fixed $c>\sqrt3$, there is an $\epsilon_c > 0$ such that our one-pass algorithm uses $\tilde O(N^{1-\epsilon_c}\poly(d))$ space, has worst-case update time $\poly(d,\log N)$, and maintains a factor-$c$ pair witness. On the hardness side, we prove that every constant-factor approximation requires polynomial memory even on short dynamic streams: a factor-$c$ approximation needs $N^{\Omega(1/(c^2\log(c+1)))}$ space on streams of at most $2N-1$ updates. Our upper bound combines a geometric hull, Gaussian hashing through successively smaller caps, and local and global rebuilding schedules. Every update changes only one leaf of the hash hierarchy, while the answer is maintained through small variance certificates. The lower bound is based on a communication complexity argument. Together, these results separate the polynomial memory regime from the time needed to process an update.
